items.stem: Which term describes the criteria journalists use to decide whether an event is newsworthy?
items.answer: News values
items.markingKey: News values: the criteria journalists use to decide whether an event is newsworthy. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “social construction of news”, and give one example.
items.answer: The idea that news is not simply a reflection of reality but is produced by organisations through selection and presentation. Example: two papers reporting the same event very differently.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the idea that news is not simply a reflection of reality but is produced by organisations through selection and presentation); 1 mark for a relevant example such as two papers reporting the same event very differently. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “social construction of news” and “framing”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Social construction of news: the idea that news is not simply a reflection of reality but is produced by organisations through selection and presentation (e.g. two papers reporting the same event very differently). Framing: the way the media present a story, highlighting some aspects and ignoring others (e.g. describing protesters as “rioters” or “campaigners”).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: On the same day, a famous footballer is arrested in Singapore and a report on rising child poverty is published; the footballer leads every news bulletin, and the report gets one line. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: media help construct social reality and labels; audiences interpret messages actively, and media reactions can amplify deviance (Cohen, Young).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: On the same day, a famous footballer is arrested in Cairo and a report on rising child poverty is published; the footballer leads every news bulletin, and the report gets one line. Explain how a pluralist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Pluralism: power in society is spread between many competing groups; the media are diverse, respond to audience demand and reflect a range of views, so no single group controls them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Karachi wants to research which types of stories appear in newspapers. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying which types of stories appear in newspapers but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: After a week of front-page stories about knife crime in Colombo, a poll finds that crime has become residents’ top concern, although recorded knife crime has fallen. Explain how Marxist and interactionist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: the media are owned and controlled by a capitalist class who use them to spread ruling-class ideology, creating false consciousness and protecting capitalism (Miliband, Murdock and Golding). Interactionism: media help construct social reality and labels; audiences interpret messages actively, and media reactions can amplify deviance (Cohen, Young).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Felix carried out a content analysis of 500 front pages from two newspapers. Table: share of front-page stories over one year (%) | Newspaper X | Newspaper Y. Crime and disasters | 26% | 26%. Celebrity and entertainment | 20% | 9%. Politics and economy | 35% | 43%. Science and development | 19% | 22%. (a) Calculate the difference between Science and development and Politics and economy for Newspaper X and for Newspaper Y, and state for which of these the difference is larger. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that news values shape what becomes news.
items.answer: (a) Newspaper X: 16 percentage points; Newspaper Y: 21 percentage points; the difference is larger for Newspaper Y. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Newspaper Y than for Newspaper X among Politics and economy, Science and development; the figure is lower for Newspaper Y than for Newspaper X among Celebrity and entertainment; Politics and economy had the highest figure for Newspaper Y. Negativity and elite persons are strong news values. Qualifications: Content analysis shows what is reported, not why; categories may overlap; online news may differ; audience demand may explain differences. The data also come from content analysis of 500 stories in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each difference (16 and 21); 1 mark for the correct comparison. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes an exaggerated public and media reaction to a group or behaviour seen as a threat to society’s values?
items.answer: Moral panic
items.markingKey: Moral panic: an exaggerated public and media reaction to a group or behaviour seen as a threat to society’s values. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “sensitisation”, and give one example.
items.answer: The process by which media coverage makes the public and police more aware of a type of deviance. Example: more reports of minor incidents after a moral panic.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the process by which media coverage makes the public and police more aware of a type of deviance); 1 mark for a relevant example such as more reports of minor incidents after a moral panic. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “moral panic” and “deviancy amplification spiral”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Moral panic: an exaggerated public and media reaction to a group or behaviour seen as a threat to society’s values (e.g. media outrage about youth gangs). Deviancy amplification spiral: the process by which media reporting increases public concern, social control and the deviance itself (e.g. more policing leading to more recorded arrests and more stories).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: Newspapers in Dubai describe migrants arriving by boat as a “flood” threatening jobs and culture; a campaign group calls for border closures. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Postmodernism: in a fragmented media world, panics are short-lived and contested; folk devils answer back through their own media (McRobbie and Thornton).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: After two fights at a music festival near Lagos, newspapers report a “wave of youth violence”; police double patrols, and arrests of young people for minor offences rise sharply. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: in a fragmented media world, panics are short-lived and contested; folk devils answer back through their own media (McRobbie and Thornton).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Newspapers in Madrid describe migrants arriving by boat as a “flood” threatening jobs and culture; a campaign group calls for border closures. Explain how interactionist and postmodernist sociologists might differ in the way they interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: the media label a group as folk devils; exaggeration and tougher control create a deviancy amplification spiral (Cohen, Young). Postmodernism: in a fragmented media world, panics are short-lived and contested; folk devils answer back through their own media (McRobbie and Thornton).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying how newspapers report youth crime.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how newspapers report youth crime but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful structured interviews are for studying how newspapers report youth crime.
items.answer: Strengths: trained interviewers can survey a large, representative sample in a standard way; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: the interviewer’s presence may produce interviewer bias or socially desirable answers; the fixed schedule cannot follow up interesting answers, so data lacks depth. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how newspapers report youth crime but best combined with another method such as content analysis (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: What is the difference between “moral entrepreneur” and “deviancy amplification spiral”?
items.answer: Moral entrepreneur: a person or group who campaigns to have a behaviour defined as deviant and controlled. Deviancy amplification spiral: the process by which media reporting increases public concern, social control and the deviance itself.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each accurate definition, showing the contrast. [2]

items.stem: A study in Kathmandu combined a content analysis of local newspapers with surveys of 600 residents, before and during a period of intense reporting of youth violence. Police figures showed little change in youth violence over the period. Table: media content and survey results in one city | Before the coverage | During the coverage. Crime stories about young people (% of all crime stories) | 24% | 57%. Residents who say youth violence is a major problem (%) | 28% | 56%. Residents who say they avoid the town centre at night (%) | 17% | 30%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Residents who say they avoid the town centre at night (%) change between Before the coverage and During the coverage?
items.answer: +13 percentage points
items.markingKey: 30 − 17 = +13 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A study in Lisbon combined a content analysis of local newspapers with surveys of 600 residents, before and during a period of intense reporting of youth violence. Police figures showed little change in youth violence over the period. Table: media content and survey results in one city | Before the coverage | During the coverage. Crime stories about young people (% of all crime stories) | 21% | 53%. Residents who say youth violence is a major problem (%) | 28% | 50%. Residents who say they avoid the town centre at night (%) | 15% | 28%. (a) Calculate the gap between Crime stories about young people (% of all crime stories) and Residents who say youth violence is a major problem (%) in Before the coverage and in During the coverage, and state whether it narrowed or widened. (b) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that moral panics exaggerate the scale of deviance.
items.answer: (a) Before the coverage: 7 percentage points; During the coverage: 3 percentage points; the gap narrowed. (b) Evidence from the data: The figure rose for Crime stories about young people (% of all crime stories), Residents who say youth violence is a major problem (%), Residents who say they avoid the town centre at night (%); Crime stories about young people (% of all crime stories) had the highest figure for During the coverage. News values such as negativity drive coverage. Qualifications: Recorded offences may under-report violence; increased policing may later raise figures; articles may reflect real public concern. The data also come from content analysis of 600 residents in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each gap (7 and 3); 1 mark for “narrowed”. [3] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses the data and own knowledge to argue for and against, with a judgement. [4]

items.stem: Which term describes herman and Chomsky’s idea that the media produce public support for the policies of powerful elites?
items.answer: Manufacture of consent
items.markingKey: Manufacture of consent: Herman and Chomsky’s idea that the media produce public support for the policies of powerful elites. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “flak”, and give one example.
items.answer: Negative responses such as complaints and lawsuits used to discipline the media. Example: a government attacking a broadcaster for a critical report.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (negative responses such as complaints and lawsuits used to discipline the media); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a government attacking a broadcaster for a critical report. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between “propaganda model” and “dominant ideology”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Propaganda model: Herman and Chomsky’s model of five filters that shape news in the interests of elites (e.g. ownership, advertising, official sources, flak and ideology). Dominant ideology: the ideas of the ruling class that are presented as natural and common sense (e.g. consumerism promoted through advertising).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A newspaper in Nairobi drops an investigation into pollution by a car manufacturer after the company threatens to withdraw its advertising. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: the media are owned and controlled by a capitalist class who use them to spread ruling-class ideology, creating false consciousness and protecting capitalism (Miliband, Murdock and Golding).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A newspaper in Manila drops an investigation into pollution by a car manufacturer after the company threatens to withdraw its advertising. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Postmodernism: media-saturated society offers endless choice; audiences actively construct identities from media images, and reality and representation blur (Baudrillard, Strinati).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Hana, a sociology student, is designing a project on how journalists respond to pressure from advertisers. Evaluate the use of unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: a sympathetic, non-judgemental interviewer can help people talk about painful or private experiences; rapport between interviewer and interviewee builds trust, so people may reveal more, producing valid data. Limitations: they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare; samples are small, so findings are difficult to generalise. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how journalists respond to pressure from advertisers but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Define the term “ideology”.
items.answer: A set of ideas and beliefs that justify the interests of a particular group.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a set of ideas and beliefs that justify the interests of a particular group. [1]

items.stem: A sociologist in Mexico City wants to research the sources quoted in news coverage of a war. Explain one limitation of using structured interviews for this research.
items.answer: The interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of the sources quoted in news coverage of a war. [2]

items.stem: In the run-up to a military intervention, TV news in Lagos relies heavily on government and military spokespeople; anti-war groups are rarely interviewed. Compare how Marxist and neo-Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Marxism: the media are owned and controlled by a capitalist class who use them to spread ruling-class ideology, creating false consciousness and protecting capitalism (Miliband, Murdock and Golding). Neo-Marxism: media content reflects ideological hegemony: journalists from similar backgrounds share middle-class, pro-establishment assumptions, so dominant values appear as common sense (Glasgow University Media Group, Hall).
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for each perspective: 1 mark for its key idea, 1 mark for applying it to the situation, 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. 1 further mark for a clear point of contrast is included within the 6. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes the power of editors and journalists to decide which stories are included or excluded?
items.answer: Gatekeeping

items.answer: Deadlines and time constraints.

items.stem: Explain Galtung and Ruge’s argument that journalists select stories according to news values such as negativity, elite persons and unexpectedness, and give one criticism of this argument.
items.answer: Galtung and Ruge identified news values that explain why some events become news. Criticism: Critics argue digital news is shaped more by clicks and algorithms.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Interactionism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.answer: 1. It records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts. 2. The researcher stays detached, so is less likely to “go native” and can record more objectively.

items.stem: A sociologist in Lima wants to research how journalists respond to pressure from advertisers. Explain two limitations of using field experiments for this research.
items.answer: 1. Deceiving people about sensitive matters may cause harm or distress. 2. Participants have not given informed consent, which raises ethical issues.

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using case studies to research how journalists respond to pressure from advertisers.
items.answer: Strengths: a single case can give rare insight into an unusual or closed group; they may use several methods, increasing validity. Limitations: the researcher’s interpretation may be biased; the detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how journalists respond to pressure from advertisers but best combined with another method such as field experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]

items.stem: Which term describes the media’s power to influence what issues the public thinks about by choosing what to cover?
items.answer: Agenda-setting
items.markingKey: Agenda-setting: the media’s power to influence what issues the public thinks about by choosing what to cover. [1]

items.stem: Define the term “news diary”.
items.answer: A list of planned events that journalists know will happen and can prepare to cover.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a list of planned events that journalists know will happen and can prepare to cover. [1]

items.stem: Explain two news values, using an example of each.
items.answer: Negativity (disasters, crime); elite persons (celebrities, leaders); proximity (local or culturally close events); unexpectedness; personalisation; threshold (size of event).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each news value; 1 mark each example. [4]

items.stem: Samuel carried out a content analysis of 500 front pages from two newspapers. Table: share of front-page stories over one year (%) | Newspaper X | Newspaper Y. Crime and disasters | 27% | 24%. Celebrity and entertainment | 16% | 13%. Politics and economy | 30% | 37%. Science and development | 27% | 26%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Newspaper X and Newspaper Y for Celebrity and entertainment (Newspaper Y minus Newspaper X)?
items.answer: -3 percentage points
items.markingKey: 13 − 16 = -3 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: After a week of front-page stories about knife crime in Cairo, a poll finds that crime has become residents’ top concern, although recorded knife crime has fallen. Explain how a neo-Marxist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Neo-Marxism: media content reflects ideological hegemony: journalists from similar backgrounds share middle-class, pro-establishment assumptions, so dominant values appear as common sense (Glasgow University Media Group, Hall).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using self-completion questionnaires to research which types of stories appear in newspapers.
items.answer: Strengths: large samples allow patterns and trends across social groups to be measured; closed, pre-coded questions produce quantitative data that is easy to compare and turn into statistics. Limitations: response rates are often low, so the sample may become unrepresentative; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying which types of stories appear in newspapers but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes a person or group who campaigns to have a behaviour defined as deviant and controlled?
items.answer: Moral entrepreneur
items.markingKey: Moral entrepreneur: a person or group who campaigns to have a behaviour defined as deviant and controlled. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “folk devil”?
items.answer: A group defined by the media as a threat to society and blamed for social problems.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a group defined by the media as a threat to society and blamed for social problems. [1]

items.stem: Explain the stages of a moral panic.
items.answer: A group or behaviour is identified as a threat; the media exaggerate and stereotype (folk devils); moral entrepreneurs demand action; authorities respond with tougher control; deviance may be amplified; the panic fades.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for each stage up to 4. [4]

items.stem: Following a few cases reported abroad, the media in Dubai warn of a dangerous online “challenge” among children; schools send letters home, and politicians demand new laws, though no local cases are found. Suggest how a neo-Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Neo-Marxism: moral panics are ideological: they create scapegoats and divert attention from crises of capitalism, justifying tougher control (Hall).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A study in Singapore combined a content analysis of local newspapers with surveys of 800 residents, before and during a period of intense reporting of youth violence. Police figures showed little change in youth violence over the period. Table: media content and survey results in one city | Before the coverage | During the coverage. Crime stories about young people (% of all crime stories) | 18% | 47%. Residents who say youth violence is a major problem (%) | 30% | 51%. Residents who say they avoid the town centre at night (%) | 16% | 29%. By how many percentage points did the figure for Residents who say youth violence is a major problem (%) change between Before the coverage and During the coverage?
items.answer: +21 percentage points
items.markingKey: 51 − 30 = +21 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: After two fights at a music festival near Auckland, newspapers report a “wave of youth violence”; police double patrols, and arrests of young people for minor offences rise sharply. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: the media label a group as folk devils; exaggeration and tougher control create a deviancy amplification spiral (Cohen, Young).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using non-participant observation to research how young people labelled as a threat respond to media coverage.
items.answer: Strengths: children can be observed in classrooms or playgrounds without having to answer questions; it records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts. Limitations: the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect); observation schedules impose the researcher’s categories on behaviour. Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how young people labelled as a threat respond to media coverage but best combined with another method such as case studies (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess the claim that the concept of moral panic is still useful for understanding the media today.
items.answer: For: Cohen and Young; recent panics about migrants, online harms, knife crime; deviancy amplification; Hall’s ideological view. Against: McRobbie and Thornton: fragmented media and media-literate audiences; folk devils fight back; concept is value-laden (who decides a reaction is disproportionate?); some concerns are justified. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on how far the view holds.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): a few simple points. Level 2 (4-6): some explained arguments, mainly on one side; limited evaluation. Level 3 (7-9): a range of explained arguments and evidence for and against, with some evaluation. Level 4 (10-12): a balanced, well-supported analysis using theories, studies and concepts, sustained evaluation and a reasoned conclusion. For: Cohen and Young; recent panics about migrants, online harms, knife crime; deviancy amplification; Hall’s ideological view. Against: McRobbie and Thornton: fragmented media and media-literate audiences; folk devils fight back; concept is value-laden (who decides a reaction is disproportionate?); some concerns are justified. [12]

items.stem: Which term describes herman and Chomsky’s model of five filters that shape news in the interests of elites?
items.answer: Propaganda model
items.markingKey: Propaganda model: Herman and Chomsky’s model of five filters that shape news in the interests of elites. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Herman and Chomsky argued the media challenge elite interests.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. They argued the media manufacture consent for elite interests.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Gramsci argued that the ruling class maintains power through hegemony, winning consent through culture and ideas. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Gramsci argued the media help make ruling-class ideas seem like common sense. Criticism: Pluralists argue there is no single dominant ideology.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Neo-Marxism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: A content analysis of 400 news reports about a conflict produced the results below. Table: share of sources quoted (%) | Television news | Online-only news sites. Government and military sources | 46% | 28%. Business sources | 16% | 12%. Campaign groups and protesters | 10% | 19%. Members of the public | 28% | 41%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Television news and Online-only news sites for Business sources (Online-only news sites minus Television news)?
items.answer: -4 percentage points
items.markingKey: 12 − 16 = -4 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: A newspaper in Mumbai drops an investigation into pollution by a car manufacturer after the company threatens to withdraw its advertising. Explain how a pluralist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Pluralism: power in society is spread between many competing groups; the media are diverse, respond to audience demand and reflect a range of views, so no single group controls them.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Amara analysed the sources quoted in 400 news reports about a war. Table: share of sources quoted (%) | Television news | Online-only news sites. Government and military sources | 46% | 28%. Business sources | 19% | 21%. Campaign groups and protesters | 10% | 24%. Members of the public | 25% | 27%. (a) Calculate the difference, in percentage points, between Television news and Online-only news sites for Members of the public. (b) Explain one reason why these data may not give a valid picture of news sources. (c) Using the data and your own sociological knowledge, evaluate the view that the news media manufacture consent for elite interests.
items.answer: (a) 27 − 25 = +2 percentage points (Online-only news sites compared with Television news). (b) Coding categories reflect the researcher’s own interpretation, so different coders may disagree. (c) Evidence from the data: The figure is higher for Online-only news sites than for Television news among Business sources, Campaign groups and protesters, Members of the public; the figure is lower for Online-only news sites than for Television news among Government and military sources; Government and military sources had the highest figure for Online-only news sites. Television relies on official sources as primary definers. Qualifications: Online sites may have their own biases; counting sources does not show how they are framed; audiences may reject official views. The data also come from content analysis of 400 news reports in one place, so they may not be representative or valid. Judgement: the data give partial support only.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for using 25 and 27; 1 mark for 2 percentage points with direction. [2] (b) 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation (validity, representativeness, reliability); 1 mark for explaining it in context. [2] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple use of data or knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): uses data AND sociological knowledge on one side, or both sides thinly. Level 3 (5-6): balanced evaluation using the data, sociological arguments and comment on the validity of the data, with a reasoned conclusion. [6]
